theme: Philip; the Samaritans; Simon the magician; the Ethiopian
readingInstruction: Read Acts 8:4-40. Persecution scatters the believers and Philip takes the gospel to Samaria and then to an Ethiopian official. Notice how the gospel crosses ethnic and social lines, and how Philip uses Isaiah 53.
settingTheScene: The persecution that began with Stephen scatters the church, and wherever they go, they preach. Philip, one of the seven, goes to Samaria, a region of mixed descent despised by Jews. This fulfills the second step of Acts 1:8. Then an angel sends him on a desert road, where he meets an Ethiopian court official, the first African convert recorded in Acts.
observation: “Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word” (8:4).
“Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ” (8:5).
“Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit” (8:17).
“May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!” (8:20).
“So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, Do you understand what you are reading?” (8:30).
“Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (8:35).
“And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing” (8:39).
“So there was much joy in that city” (8:8).
interpretation:
Persecution scatters the church, but the believers go about preaching the word. What the enemy meant for harm, God used to spread the gospel. Philip goes to Samaria and proclaims Christ. The crowds pay attention as they see signs: unclean spirits come out, and the paralyzed and lame are healed. “So there was much joy in that city.” The long hostility between Jews and Samaritans begins to heal in Christ.

A man named Simon had amazed the Samaritans with magic, claiming to be someone great. He believes and is baptized, but later, when he sees the Spirit given through the laying on of hands by Peter and John, he offers money for the power. Peter replies sharply: “Your heart is not right before God. Repent.” Christians differ on whether Simon’s faith was genuine. The main lesson is that the gift of God cannot be bought, and the heart must be right.

The apostles Peter and John come from Jerusalem to the Samaritans, who had been baptized but had not yet received the Spirit. When they lay hands on them, the Spirit comes. This is an unusual sequence, and interpreters explain it as a special moment as the gospel crossed a boundary: the Samaritans received the Spirit in the presence of the apostles, so that the Jerusalem church would recognize them as full members. It is not the usual pattern, where the Spirit comes with faith (Romans 8:9).

An angel directs Philip to a desert road. He meets an Ethiopian court official, treasurer of the queen, who has been to Jerusalem to worship and is returning in his chariot, reading Isaiah 53. Philip asks, “Do you understand what you are reading?” “How can I, unless someone guides me?” The passage is the suffering servant, led like a sheep to the slaughter. “About whom does the prophet say this?” Philip begins with this Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus. The man asks to be baptized in some water they pass. After the baptism, the Spirit takes Philip away, and the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing. Tradition holds that he carried the gospel to Africa.

The gospel is moving. It reached Samaritans, who were half-Jewish, and now an African who was excluded from the temple assembly under the law (Deuteronomy 23:1) but who is welcomed in Christ, as Isaiah 56:3-5 promised.
connection: Isaiah 53:7-8 is the passage the Ethiopian was reading. Isaiah 56:3-5 promises a place for eunuchs in God’s house. Psalm 68:31 says Cush will stretch out its hands to God. John 4:1-42 shows Jesus ministering in Samaria. Luke 9:51-56 shows earlier Samaritan hostility. 1 Peter 1:10-12 says the prophets searched for the sufferings of Christ. Luke 24:27 and 24:45 show Jesus opening the Scriptures. Romans 10:14-15 says how can they hear without someone preaching.
application:
Ask a friend about what they are reading, and be ready like Philip to explain from Scripture.

Notice whom your culture excludes. How could you bring the gospel to them?

Thank God that persecution cannot stop his word.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for using hard things to spread his word.
Ask him to make you willing to go where he sends.
Ask him to open your eyes to someone who is seeking.
